issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a rape trauma profile, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is the only item that implies perpetration or morally troubling behaviour by the patient. Paired with memory items centered on terror and shame and trigger items tied to tiredness, driving with others, and sounds, this appraisal is hard to reconcile clinically with the rest of the profile and with the trauma type. The other negative appraisals reflect mistrust and loss of faith, which fit sexual assault trauma; this item instead points toward a different moral injury formulation and creates an internal mismatch within the Negative Appraisals node.

vignette: Rafael Hernandez had been driving a bus for over two decades, but it wasn't until after the night he was brutally raped by a stranger that every route started to feel like a minefield. The slightest sound – the creak of a seat, the rustle of clothes – would transport him back to that dark alley, his heart racing with the same terror he felt at the time. Feeling tired or exhausted, which had become an all-too-familiar state for Rafael, also seemed to trigger these memories, as if his body was too worn down to keep them at bay. As he drove, Rafael couldn't shake off the feeling that people couldn't be trusted – a mistrust that extended even to his own passengers. He would catch himself wondering what each person on the bus might be capable of, and it made him feel ashamed of his own vulnerability. The memory replayed in his mind like a film: the sound of footsteps behind him, the hand covering his mouth, the feeling of being completely overpowered. This shame was not just about what happened to his body but also about how he perceived himself – weak, powerless. Rafael had lost faith in people and life itself; it seemed that anyone could be a potential threat. Even his wife's touch would sometimes startle him, reminding him of the stranger's hands on his skin. The memories came flooding back, and with them, the same intense shame he felt at the time. Rafael became convinced that his body was tainted by what had happened, that it was somehow less worthy because of the violence inflicted upon it. As a result, Rafael started to avoid driving routes that took him through areas that reminded him of the alley where the assault occurred. He also began to dread having people sit near him on the bus, especially if they were loud or boisterous. The sounds they made would set off a chain reaction in his mind, leading him back to the memory of that night and reinforcing his mistrust of others. Rafael's wife noticed the change in him – how withdrawn he had become, how easily startled – and encouraged him to seek help. But Rafael was afraid of what therapy might uncover, of reliving those memories again. He felt like he was drowning in a sea of triggers, each one threatening to pull him under into the darkness of that night. It wasn't until Rafael had a particularly distressing episode on the job – where a passenger's loud laughter triggered a full-blown flashback – that he realized he needed help to break this cycle. He couldn't keep living like this, constantly on edge, waiting for the next trigger to send him spiraling back into the past. With his wife's support, Rafael made an appointment with a therapist, hoping to find a way to quiet the memories and rebuild his faith in himself and others.
